newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine C. Bank stretched thin in peso defence.
newsitem.headline: Philippine C. Bank stretched thin in peso defence.

text.p: The Philippine Central Bank may be stretching itself too thin in its bid to protect the peso from speculation inspired by the Thai baht's troubles, economists said on Tuesday.
Defence of the currency, which has been hammered by fears of spillover from Thailand's financial crisis, has already forced interest rates up and begun to drain gross international reserves.
"They can't keep doing intervention," said Far East Bank economist Emma Pante.
"They're eating up gross international reserves which aren't that big and which only cover the mandatory three months' worth of imports."
She noted the cost of corporate borrowing had also gone up.
Far East Bank itself had raised its short-term prime lending rate to 16 percent from 14 percent last Friday.

The Philippine Central Bank in recent months had to raise its closely-watched overnight borrowing rate several times to defend the peso from speculators who saw the economy going down the same path as Thailand.
Thailand is suffering from a slumping stock market, an ailing property sector which has saddled banks with bad loans, and repeated speculative attacks on its currency, the baht.
The speculation forced the Thai government to change its exchange rate system on July 2 to a "managed float", effectively devaluing the baht.
The Thai situation and subsequent attacks on the peso have prompted fears of a similar peso devaluation forced by speculators.

The uncertainty surrounding the peso was underscored when a Singapore newspaper report, subsequently denied by Philippine officials, quoted Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo as saying devaluation was possible.

Peso trading surged on the report and the central bank on Monday had to raise interest rates six percentage points to 30 percent, the highest since the last wave of attacks on the currency after the Mexican peso crisis 2-1/2 years ago.
Some analysts said the peso also needed to fall in line with last week's de facto devaluation of the Thai baht to keep local products competitive in the world market.
Analysts also said if the Central Bank wants to lower interest rates it would have to allow a depreciation of the peso.
Philippine exporters also have been pressing for a gradual depreciation to make exports more competitive.
"Without the external difficulty, we were looking at a year-end rate of 26.75 pesos (to the dollar) or less than two percent depreciation," the chief analyst of a foreign brokerage house said.
Over a period of two years, the peso could have slowly depreciated to 27.50/28.00 pesos, the analyst said. But in the current situation, "it might be over a short time."
The rate is currently around 26.38 pesos to the dollar.
Some bank officials say the Central Bank may give in to the calls for a peso depreciation but a big move is unlikely.
"What is required by the fundamentals is only a slight movement of the currency, not a sharp movement," said Ropi Dangazo, strategic planning and research head of Union Bank of the Philippines.
"This is just a hiccup. Things will return to normal," he stressed, adding that the Central Bank can always call on the help of other Asian central banks.

Late last week, the Central Bank said the level of foreign currency deposits in the country, which were at $16.58 billion as of June 20 from the year-earlier $11.73 billion, added to the peso's stability.
It said the foreign exchange deposits, mostly from export earnings and remittances from overseas workers, are considered a secondary buffer in the country's foreign exchange needs.
The Central Bank, however, has not reported its latest gross international reserves since mid-May.
